source: Shen et al. (2026) Decocted Experience Improves Test-Time Inference in LLM Agents
finding: Distilled lessons from past trajectories work better than raw stored experience for math and agent tasks. Performance has a sweet spot at intermediate memory size that can beat the full memory. More memory is not always better.
numbers: Seed-OSS-36B-Instruct (GPT-OSS-20B extension). Math: AMC23, AIME24, AIME25, HMMT24, HMMT25, BeyondAIME (260 test problems), memory from DAPO-Math. WebShop: 200 test episodes, 3,930 training trajectories. SWE-bench Verified: 500 instances, 1,794 training instances. Top-K retrieval K=8 (math), K=4 (WebShop, SWE).
quote: We show that effective context construction critically depends on decocted experience.
limits: The page text gives no exact numbers for the memory-size curve (figure only). No equal-token control stated; efficiency is output length and step count. No log-law fit.
agent_relevance: Evidence against a simple 'more solved cases, better' law: expect a plateau or sweet spot. Distilled, consolidated chunks beat raw logs.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: experience-following behavior
finding: Agents copy outputs of the most similar stored case (experience-following). Adding every case hurts; adding only checked-good cases helps; deleting some old cases can help.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini main. Add-all vs fixed memory (perf / memory size): RegAgent 55.48/4100 vs 67.53/100; EHRAgent 13.05/2411 vs 16.75/100; AgentDriver 32.32/2125 vs 40.11/180; CIC-IoT 59.90/1050 vs 71.50/50. Strict (oracle) addition: 70.95, 38.50, 51.00, 85.40. Deletion: EHRAgent history-based 42.06 at 784 records vs 38.67 at 1,012 with no deletion. Pearson r near 1 between input and output similarity in RegAgent.
quote: Conversely, indiscriminate memory addition will easily introduce incorrect executions for the agent to learn from
limits: Four tasks, mostly GPT-4o-mini. Memory size measured in records, not tokens. Quality of the library, not size, drives results.
agent_relevance: A case library is only as good as its admission rule. Gate chunks on verified success; expect errors to propagate by near-copying.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners (AAAI)
finding: Agents that collect experiences and extract insights improve on HotpotQA over ReAct. The ablation says autonomously collected experiences are essential, not just the few-shot examples.
numbers: HotpotQA success: ReAct 28.0 +-1.4% vs ExpeL 39.0 +-1.7% (gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 agent, gpt-4-0613 for insight extraction).
limits: Fetched text gave no numeric curve for number of training tasks (Figure 6 is an image) and no equal-token control. So the log-law question is not answered by this paper.
agent_relevance: Supports gain from stored cases, but gives no scaling law or token-matched test.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-Shot In-Context Learning
finding: Giving hundreds to thousands of examples in context beats few-shot, but gains are not monotone. Some tasks peak and then decline. Repeating a few examples does not help.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Pro. MATH standard ICL peaks near 125 shots then declines; reinforced ICL plateaus near 25 shots (about +5%). XSum peaks near 50 shots. GPQA: 125 shots beats 40.4% reference, declines at 250. Bemba translation +15.3% with 997 examples (about 85K tokens). Repeating 25 examples to 1,000 shots is nearly flat. Planning (Logistics) 42% to 62%.
limits: Fixed demonstrations, not a retrieved case library; many-shot costs many tokens, so it is not equal-token. Paper has no retrieval comparison.
agent_relevance: Indirect analogue: returns to library size are task-dependent and can turn negative. Distinct examples matter, not repeats.

source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Trapped in the past? Disentangling fluid and crystallized intelligence of LLMs using chess (re-opened for gap 2)
finding: Re-read for gap 2: only chess was tested. The authors speculate the pattern extends to math and software synthesis but do not test it. Reasoning helps less per token the further from training data.
numbers: 500 positions per condition (WD, ND, OOD), 1,500 total; GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5 (minimal, moderate). Avg CPL 807.97 / 540.38 / 463.5; legal-move rate 25.3 / 58.4 / 66.2%. GPT-5 moderate reasoning tokens about 3,426 (WD), 11,800 (ND), 16,953 (OOD); CPL gain per token 9.9e-4, 4.92e-4, 1.13e-4. Illegal moves 1.46x (ND) and 4.72x (OOD) vs WD.
quote: Our results reveal a consistent performance gradient: accuracy declines as the need for OOD generalization increases.
limits: No non-chess task, no scaffold arm, no equal-token comparison across scaffolds. Responses Aug-Oct 2025.
agent_relevance: The OOD collapse is not shown outside chess. Our scaffold's effect on it is untested, so run an OOD-split test on non-chess tasks.

source: Zhao et al. (2025) Is Chain-of-Thought Reasoning of LLMs a Mirage? A Data Distribution Lens
finding: Controlled from-scratch training environment (DataAlchemy). CoT reasoning breaks when task, length or format shifts away from the training distribution. This is a non-chess OOD collapse, but on small synthetic models.
numbers: Abstract only read; the numeric results were not available in the fetched page.
quote: CoT reasoning is a brittle mirage when it is pushed beyond training distributions
limits: Abstract only; models are trained from scratch, not frontier LLMs. Do not quote numbers.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that OOD brittleness is not only a chess effect, though evidence is synthetic.

source: Qian et al. (2026) AI4AI at Test-Time: Strong-to-Weak Capability Transfer via Harnesses (Salesforce)
finding: Scaffolds built by a strong model lift a weak target a lot but a strong target little, and can hurt a strong target on tasks it already does well. Uplift follows headroom.
numbers: Four Theory-of-Mind benchmarks. GPT-5.4-mini 0.488 to 0.750 (+0.262); Gemini-3.5-flash 0.761 to 0.871 (+0.110). Uplift vs headroom (1-baseline) Pearson r=0.75. Gemini gain 96% on BigToM. No regression for GPT-5.4-mini (0/20 builder-benchmark cases); for Gemini every builder regressed on at least one benchmark (9/20): Hi-ToM -0.04, MuMA-ToM -0.02 on average.
quote: when the target is already close to ceiling, additional prompts, routing, or rules may disrupt correct behavior more often than they repair errors
limits: Preprint, one task family (Theory of Mind), two targets, three repeats per builder. Regressions small. Not token-matched.
agent_relevance: Direct scaffold analogue of expertise reversal: scale guardrail strength to headroom. On familiar, near-ceiling tasks use a light scaffold.

source: Independent author (2025) You Don't Need Prompt Engineering Anymore: The Prompting Inversion (arXiv 2510.22251)
finding: On GSM8K a constrained prompt ('sculpting') beat plain CoT on weaker models but lost to CoT on GPT-5. Small and single-run.
numbers: Accuracy zero-shot / CoT / sculpting, N=100: gpt-4o-mini 86/91/93; gpt-4o 88/93/97; gpt-5 97/99/97. Full gpt-5, N=1,317: 94.00 / 96.36 / 94.00.
quote: We studied only OpenAI's GPT models.
limits: Only GSM8K, only OpenAI models, temperature 0, one query each, no confidence intervals. The 100-item gaps are within noise; the 1,317 GPT-5 gap (2.4 points) is the firmer part.
agent_relevance: Weak support that rigid constraints can cost accuracy on a strong model. Needs replication.

source: Basil, Shapiro, Shapiro, Mollick, Mollick, Meincke (2025) Prompting Science Report 4: Playing Pretend: Expert Personas Don't Improve Factual Accuracy
finding: Expert personas, matched or mismatched, did not reliably raise accuracy on hard multiple-choice questions. Low-knowledge personas often lowered it. This repeats b25 with different models and benchmarks.
numbers: Six models: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o3-mini, o4-mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Flash. GPQA Diamond: 198 questions x 25 runs = 4,950 runs per model-prompt. MMLU-Pro subset: 300 questions, 7,500 runs. GPQA: only significant gain was Young Child on Gemini 2.5 Flash (risk difference 0.098, p=0.005). MMLU-Pro: five of six models no expert gain, nine significant negative differences; Gemini 2.0 Flash exception (Engineering Expert vs baseline RD 0.089, p=0.002).
limits: Role labels only; no domain facts were supplied in the prompts. Accuracy only.
agent_relevance: Do not use role labels as a knowledge substitute. Knowledge must be given as content (retrieved facts or cases).

source: Xiao et al. (2026) When Does Persona Prompting Actually Help? A Retrieval and Metric Analysis of Expert Role Injection
finding: Retrieving a better expert role prompt did not beat no role. Role prompts raised expertise depth but cut clarity. This retrieves role prompts, not domain facts.
numbers: 1,140 open-ended questions, 38 roles, 6 domains, GPT-4o mini answerer, Claude Haiku 4.5 judge. Mean scores: baseline 4.390, hybrid retrieval 4.382, general expert 4.373, embedding retrieval 4.349. Friedman chi2=31.30, p=7.3e-7; all Cohen's d < 0.12.
limits: LLM judge, one answering model, independent authors. Does not test persona plus domain facts.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: no study pairs persona with real domain facts. Role selection adds little.

source: Gong, Ericsson, Moxley (2015) Recall of briefly presented chess positions (re-opened for gap 8)
finding: Two ways to count chunks (timing, and repeated recall) agree highly but test-retest reliability of chunk count is modest and differs by method.
numbers: Correlation between the two techniques 0.85 or higher on all boards. Test-retest for number of chunks on game positions: .65 (repeated-recall) vs .36 (timing), significantly different; among rated players .60 vs .36. For random positions about .14. 25 rated players, 25 non-players.
limits: Small sample; reliability low for random boards. Chunk count is noisy.
agent_relevance: Do not use chunk count as the agent metric. Use task accuracy gap (structured vs scrambled) averaged over many items.

source: Chassy and Gobet (2011) Measuring chess experts' single-use sequence knowledge: archival study of departures from theoretical openings (PLoS ONE)
finding: Direct estimate from 76,562 games: masters know about 100,000 opening moves. The paper also lists the older chunk estimates, which were indirect simulation figures.
numbers: 76,562 games played in 2008, Class B to Master. Simon and Gilmartin proposed 10,000 to 100,000 chunks; Gobet and Simon proposed as many as 300,000. Chassy and Gobet: about 100,000 opening moves for masters.
limits: Opening moves are single-use rote knowledge, a different thing from perceptual chunks. Branching-factor assumption drives the estimate.
agent_relevance: Reconciles gap 5: store size is 10^4 to 3x10^5 depending on method; 50,000 is the middle. Size matters less than retrieval by cue.

source: Connors, Burns, Campitelli (2011) Expertise in complex decision making: the role of search in chess 70 years after de Groot (Cognitive Science)
finding: Replication of de Groot's think-aloud study. Skill differences in search speed, no big change in the pattern-recognition conclusion.
numbers: 6 Grandmasters, 5 International Masters, 6 Experts, 5 Class A players; two positions each. GMs and IMs search faster than Experts and Class A; both search substantially faster than players in earlier studies.
limits: Only the abstract was read (via Europe PMC). Small N.
agent_relevance: Backs the template story: experts get to a good move quickly via recognition. It does not change the schema.

source: McGrath et al. (2022) Acquisition of chess knowledge in AlphaZero (PNAS)
finding: A network trained only by self-play, with no human games, comes to hold many human chess concepts. Probes show concepts appear in a staged way, and most concept computation sits in early layers.
numbers: 1 million training steps, batch 4,096, network refreshed every 1,000 steps. Concept regression accuracy rises sharply near 32k steps (32,000) and then plateaus past block depth about 10. Opening analysis with a former world champion.
limits: Interpretability and qualitative opening review; no recall experiment, no random-board test. Not about LLMs.
agent_relevance: Supports that concept-like chunks can be learned without human labels, but it does not change the agent schema: concept acquisition story stays as before.

source: Scrambled Bench (2023) Unveiling LLM scrambled text recovery (arXiv 2311.18805)
finding: GPT-4 almost fully reconstructs scrambled sentences and answers questions over scrambled context. This scrambles letters inside words, not the structure of the task, so it is a weak analogue of random chess boards.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot recovery rate on RealtimeQA: 93.76 (20% scrambled), 95.89 (50%), 95.94 (100%). Scrambled QA relative performance gain: 99.19, 97.56, 87.80. RealtimeQA 418 recovery and 346 QA samples; DREAM 1,025.
quote: GPT-4 can recover sentences by 95% edit distance reduction even in 100% randomly scrambling settings.
limits: Within-word letter scrambling. No expert-novice comparison. Language is highly redundant.
agent_relevance: A text-level shuffle does not reproduce the human recall gap; use structure-level shuffles (shuffled steps, shuffled code lines).

finding: Reordering the characters of fixed four-character expressions is hard for twelve LLMs. Exact recovery is far from perfect even with reasoning.
numbers: 3,543 expressions x 23 permutations = 81,489 inputs, twelve LLMs. Zero-shot recovery from 12.167% (Llama-3-8B) to 31.062% (Qwen-3-14B); with chain-of-thought DeepSeek-V3.2 reaches 62.238%.
quote: Exact reconstruction is difficult even for strong systems.
limits: No numeric drop from unshuffled input given in the read text (appendix cut off). CJK idioms only.
agent_relevance: Order and structure shuffles do hurt, so the structured-vs-shuffled gap can be measured on structured inputs, but it has not been done as a skill-graded recall test.
